title: Sunrise on the Reaping may be a prequel, but it's the worst way to start The Hunger Games
summary: The framing of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping as a painful, nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone…

image.caption: Joseph Zada as a young Haymitch Abernathy in a still from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. (Murray Close/Lionsgate)

blocks.text: Entertainment·REVIEW

The framing of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping as a painful, nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone feature.
Latest chapter in dystopian franchise is more focused on backstory than story — and is almost absurdly morose
There is perhaps no worse instalment of The Hunger Games franchise to get started with than the new prequel, Sunrise on the Reaping.

That should be a silly statement on face value. With five movies in the young-adult, Battle Royale-esque series already out — four of them following "girl on fire" Katniss Everdeen's quest to stop the dictatorial Capitol government from pitting randomly selected kids against one another in modern gladiator matches — you'd think the audience is coming in fairly well versed.

So with Sunrise on the Reaping simply moving back and telling the story of how one grizzled character once competed in a blood-soaked tournament of his own, why does The Hunger Games need to hold your hand?

Well, because its creator said that was the goal. According to director Francis Lawrence, making Reaping function as a genuine entry point into the series works for both new and old audiences, independent of their experience with other films — a claim to craft a functional and entertaining midbrow action movie with new faces, but also to make it stand entirely on its own merits.
It's a lofty pair of goals — the first of which Reaping actually more or less meets as a relatively strong entry in the overcrowded, clichéd YA post-apocalyptic canon.
But in confronting the second goal, it ends up either failing outright; or barely passes by crafting one of the more bizarrely morose entries in the "chosen one" narrative field of all time.

Instead of introducing the undauntable, constantly thwarted heroine Katniss, we follow the battle-scarred side character of Haymitch Abernathy — whose function has long been to be unhappy — and are told what made him so titillatingly broken when fans first met him.
That might be interesting for those who have followed along from the beginning and are just hungry for more.

But to those without any insight into who eventually triumphs over whom decades after all this unrewarding, unrelenting, unromantic failure, Reaping is something else. Its framing as a painful, almost universally nihilistic and unrelentingly dour backstory for a single character makes it a deeply strange movie when viewed as a standalone feature.

Played in the original Hunger Games by Woody Harrelson as a grizzled, traumatized veteran of the games, Haymitch is here taken on by Joseph Zada. It's 24 years ahead of the events of the first movie, on the eve of something called the Second Quarter Quell.

It is a requisitely arcane term for a pivotal Hunger Games competition, one that those following along know ended in even more bloodshed and tears than is normal — and somehow left an older, meaner Haymitch looking on in fiery-eyed fury when the corrupt, manipulative government presented him with doctored, propagandistic footage of it in the first movie.
For those out of the know, though, this movie could still end in either heroic victory or heroic martyrization.

Those expectations seem even more likely as we go through the typical setup: music video shots of Haymitch telling his girl Lenore (Whitney Peak) in a slightly southern accent that he'll never let her go; Haymitch saving her from his fate by selflessly setting himself up "tribute" for his district — the saddest, rinky-dinkiest, underdoggiest district in the whole state of Panem; and his ironic slow-clapping at the impassive President Snow (Ralph Fiennes) looking down at the moaning and dying young combatants in the arena below.
Ralph Fiennes as President Snow in a still from The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping. (Lionsgate)

These are all expected and solidly executed moral and narrative markers for the tragic or triumphant formula to work off. They get more narrative juice once the real plot starts, as the mysterious Beetee Latier (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) sneaks out from the arena compound's shadows to present Haymitch with a plan to take the Capitol down from the inside, forgo trying to win the competition, and try to stop the ruling class from exploiting them.
There's only one problem: if Haymitch does this, he's not getting out alive.

Of course, this being the backstory for a character still alive in other Hunger Games movies precludes that eventuality. But instead of ruining the experience for those who know the broad-strokes ending, it only diminishes it: what was once compellingly mysterious, hinted-at trauma in Haymitch's rear-mirror moves from imagination and suggestion to about 30 minutes of screaming, montage-based alcoholism and more tiny coffins than a Dracula-themed dollhouse.

Where the maudlin collage of trauma in Reaping's back half might harden and simplify old fans' relationship with Haymitch, it is simply bizarre for a newcomer. Instead of a story about victory over fascism — either real, performative or pyrrhic — we get a cruel rug-pull that lacks both a cohesive emotional framing and message.

blocks.text: A fuzzy theme around learned helplessness is there — the "implicit submission" of the masses obeying a minority explained by philosopher David Hume, as The Hunger Games author Suzanne Collins has said. And, sure, the citizens in Reaping fail to realize the power they have to fight back.

But aside from a trite, tacked-on ending — whose emotional weight hinges entirely upon the assumption you know the triumphs Katniss Everdeen will achieve — the rest is just punishment for punishment's sake.

The dragged-out, morose portrayal of the pointlessness of Haymitch's existence works to explain his later anger — a useful tidbit if you ever make it to the first film. But aside from the novelty of a story refusing you redemption or fulfillment, there's little else for those making their way into the tale.
With the real end to Sunrise on the Reaping being The Hunger Games, you might as well start there. Or not start at all.
